Proposition 3.4 is said to be 'essentially contained in' Kuwabara [Ku90] but in a narrower case; Hard rule 3 is ambiguous here, kept origin paper.
'Notation and Remarks' 2.2 mixes standard notation with remarks on Kaluza-Klein reduction and self-adjointness; typed definition.
Pesce's strong isospectrality theorem and its definitions are stated inside the proof of Proposition 3.7 and kept as proof steps rather than separate external nodes.
The introduction's informal statement of the main theorem and the definition of Spec(L,nabla,k) are restated later (Theorem 3.6, Notation 3.3); only the later copies are nodes.

nodes.statement_short: The bundle Laplacian is minus the trace of the second covariant derivative.
nodes.label: BundleLaplacian

nodes.name: Does quantum equivalence imply classical equivalence?
nodes.statement: Does the collection of all $Spec(L,{\nabla},k)$, $k\in{\mathbb{Z}}$, determine the symplectic structure $\Omega$ on $T^*M$? That is, does ``quantum equivalence'' of two magnetic fields imply their ``classical equivalence''?
nodes.statement_short: Do the spectra of all tensor powers of the line bundle determine the magnetic symplectic structure on $T^*M$?

nodes.name: Kuwabara's isospectral connections on a fixed line bundle
nodes.statement: Our technique is similar to that of R. Kuwabara \cite{Ku90}, who constructed pairs of connections on a fixed line bundle $L$ over, for example, a Riemann surface $M$ such that $Spec(L,{\nabla}_1,k)=Spec(L,{\nabla}_2,k)$ for all $k$.
assumptions: a fixed line bundle $L$ over, for example, a Riemann surface $M$
nodes.statement_short: Kuwabara constructed pairs of connections on a fixed line bundle isospectral for all tensor powers.

nodes.name: Magnetic field (closed 2-form)
nodes.statement: In analogy with the situation in ${\mathbb{R}}^3$, a closed 2-form $\omega$ on a Riemannian manifold $(M,g)$ can be interpreted as a magnetic field.
nodes.section: 2.1 Hamiltonian system associated with a magnetic field

nodes.name: Magnetic phase space symplectic form
nodes.statement: The Hamiltonian system for a charged particle moving in the magnetic field has phase space $(T^{\ast}M, \Omega)$ with $\Omega:=\omega_{0}+\pi^{\ast}\omega$, where $\omega_{0}$ is the Liouville form on $T^*M$ (that is, $\omega_0=-d\lambda$, where $\lambda$ is the canonical $1$-form on the cotangent bundle), and $\pi:T^{\ast}M\rightarrow M$ is the projection; see \cite{GSS}, for example.
nodes.section: 2.1 Hamiltonian system associated with a magnetic field
nodes.statement_short: The magnetic phase space is $T^*M$ with twisted symplectic form $\Omega=\omega_0+\pi^*\omega$.

nodes.name: Kinetic energy Hamiltonian
nodes.statement: The classical trajectories of the particle are given by the Hamiltonian flow of the (kinetic energy) Hamiltonian $H(q,\xi):=\frac{1}{2}g_q(\xi,\xi)$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Hamiltonian system associated with a magnetic field

nodes.name: Classical equivalence
nodes.statement: We will say that $(M_1,g_1,\omega_1)$ and $(M_2,g_2,\omega_2)$ are \emph{classically equivalent} if the associated Hamiltonian systems $(T^{\ast}M_1, \Omega_1, H_1)$ and $(T^{\ast}M_2, \Omega_2, H_2)$ are equivalent.
nodes.section: 2.1 Hamiltonian system associated with a magnetic field
differentia: the associated Hamiltonian systems $(T^{\ast}M_1, \Omega_1, H_1)$ and $(T^{\ast}M_2, \Omega_2, H_2)$ are equivalent
nodes.label: ce

nodes.name: Prequantum line bundle, Kaluza-Klein metric and bundle Laplacians
nodes.section: 2.1 Hamiltonian system associated with a magnetic field
nodes.statement_short: Line bundle $L$ with Chern class $[\omega/2\pi]$ and connection of curvature $-i\omega$; its circle bundle with Kaluza-Klein metric; the Laplacian on $L^{\otimes k}$ and the $L^2$ Hilbert space.
nodes.label: prep

nodes.name: Geometric quantization of the magnetic Hamiltonian
nodes.statement: \cite[p. 204]{Woo} We use Notation~\ref{prep} and assume that $[\omega/2\pi]$ is an integral cohomology class. The quantum Hilbert space associated to the classical Hamiltonian system $(T^{\ast}M,\Omega,H)$ of Subsection~\ref{class} is given for each integer $k$ by $\mathcal{H}_{k}=L^{2}(M,L^{\otimes k})$ (the space of square-integrable sections of ${L^{\otimes k}}$) and the quantization of the Hamiltonian $H$ is the (unbounded) operator \begin{equation} \widehat{H}_{k}=-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2}(-\Delta-\tfrac{1}{6}R) \end{equation} on $\mathcal{H}_{k}$, where $R$ is the scalar curvature of the metric $g$. (Here $\hbar= \frac{1}{k})$.
conclusions: The quantum Hilbert space associated to the classical Hamiltonian system $(T^{\ast}M,\Omega,H)$ of Subsection~\ref{class} is given for each integer $k$ by $\mathcal{H}_{k}=L^{2}(M,L^{\otimes k})$ (the space of square-integrable sections of ${L^{\otimes k}}$)

the quantization of the Hamiltonian $H$ is the (unbounded) operator \begin{equation} \widehat{H}_{k}=-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2}(-\Delta-\tfrac{1}{6}R) \end{equation} on $\mathcal{H}_{k}$, where $R$ is the scalar curvature of the metric $g$. (Here $\hbar= \frac{1}{k})$.
nodes.statement_short: The quantum Hilbert space is $L^2(M,L^{\otimes k})$ and the quantum Hamiltonian is $-\frac{\hbar^2}{2}(-\Delta-\frac16 R)$ with $\hbar=1/k$.
nodes.label: hk

nodes.name: Quantum Hamiltonian
nodes.statement: \widehat{H}_{k}=-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2}(-\Delta-\tfrac{1}{6}R)
nodes.label: Hamiltonian

nodes.name: Dependence on choice of connection
nodes.statement: The definition of the Laplacian $\Delta$ on ${L^{\otimes k}}$, and thus of the operators $\widehat{H}_{k}$, depends on a choice of connection on $L$ with the specified curvature~$-i\omega$. However, in the examples that we will give in Subsection~\ref{ex}, there will be a natural choice of connection with that curvature.
nodes.label: amb

nodes.name: Quantum equivalence
nodes.statement: Let ($M_i, g_i)$, $i=1,2$, be a compact Riemannian manifold and let $\omega_i$ be a closed $2$-form on $M_i$ such that $[\omega/2\pi]$ is an integral cohomology class. For each integer $k$, let $\widehat{H}_{k}^i:L^{2}(M,L_i^{\otimes k})\rightarrow L^{2}(M,L_i^{\otimes k})$ be the associated quantum Hamiltonian as given in Theorem~\ref{hk}. We will say that $(M_1, \omega_1)$ and $(M_2,\omega_2)$ are \emph{quantum equivalent} (with respect to the connections used to define the line bundle Laplacians) if for every $k$, the operators $\widehat{H}_{k}^1$ and $\widehat{H}_{k}^2$ have the same spectrum.
differentia: for every $k$, the operators $\widehat{H}_{k}^1$ and $\widehat{H}_{k}^2$ have the same spectrum
nodes.statement_short: Two magnetic fields are quantum equivalent if their quantum Hamiltonians have the same spectrum for every $k$.
nodes.label: qe

nodes.name: Outline of geometric quantization (derivation of Theorem 2.3)
nodes.statement_short: Outline of geometric quantization: prequantization via Kostant-Souriau, vertical polarization, BKS half-form correction. The quantum Hamiltonian is the $t$-derivative of the BKS-projected evolved prequantum flow.

nodes.name: Kostant-Souriau prequantum operator
nodes.statement: \widehat{f}^{preQ}:=\frac{i}{k}\nabla_{X_{f}}^{L_{\Omega}^{\otimes k} }+f,
nodes.label: eqn:K-Squantization

nodes.name: Dirac's quantization conditions for Kostant-Souriau prequantization
nodes.statement: The Kostant--Souriau prequantization (\ref{eqn:K-Squantization}) satisfies Dirac's quantization conditions: \begin{enumerate} \item the map $f\mapsto\widehat{f}$ $^{preQ}$is linear, \item the quantization $\widehat{1}^{preQ}$ of the constant map $1$ is the identity operator, and \item $[\widehat{f}^{preQ},\widehat{g}^{preQ}]=-i\hbar\widehat{\{f,g\}}^{preQ},$ where $\{\cdot,\cdot\}$ is the Poisson bracket, $[\cdot,\cdot]$ is the operator commutator, and $\hbar=1/k$. \end{enumerate}
conclusions: the quantization $\widehat{1}^{preQ}$ of the constant map $1$ is the identity operator
nodes.statement_short: Kostant-Souriau prequantization is linear, sends 1 to the identity, and maps Poisson brackets to commutators.

nodes.name: Half-form pairing
nodes.statement: \langle s\nu,t\nu\rangle = \left(\frac{k}{2\pi}\right)^n\int_M s.t\ \operatorname{vol}_g(M).
nodes.label: eqn:half-form-pairing

nodes.name: Prequantum line bundle on phase space
nodes.statement_short: Pull back $L$ and its connection to $T^*M$ to get a connection of curvature $-i\Omega$.

nodes.name: Prequantization and Kostant-Souriau operator
nodes.statement: The \emph{prequantization} of the Hamiltonian system $(T^{\ast}M,\Omega)$ is the space of square-integrable sections of $L_{\Omega}^{\otimes k}$ with respect to the standard inner product \[ \langle s,t\rangle:=\left( \frac{k}{2\pi}\right) ^{n}\int_{T^{\ast}M}s.t~\frac{\Omega^{n}}{n!}, \] where $s.t$ denotes the (pointwise) Hermitian product on $L_{\Omega}^{\otimes k}.$ For a smooth function $f$ on $T^*M$ (we are interested in particular in the Hamiltonian $H$ above), one associates a \emph{prequantum Hamiltonian operator} $\widehat{f}^{preQ}$, given by the Kostant--Souriau construction: \begin{equation} \widehat{f}^{preQ}:=\frac{i}{k}\nabla_{X_{f}}^{L_{\Omega}^{\otimes k} }+f, \end{equation} where $X_{f}$ is the Hamiltonian vector field associated to $f$, defined by $\Omega(X_{f},\cdot)=df(\cdot)$.
nodes.statement_short: Define the prequantum Hilbert space and the Kostant-Souriau prequantum operators.

nodes.name: Dirac's quantization conditions
nodes.statement: The Kostant--Souriau prequantization (\ref{eqn:K-Squantization}) satisfies Dirac's quantization conditions: \begin{enumerate} \item the map $f\mapsto\widehat{f}$ $^{preQ}$is linear, \item the quantization $\widehat{1}^{preQ}$ of the constant map $1$ is the identity operator, and \item $[\widehat{f}^{preQ},\widehat{g}^{preQ}]=-i\hbar\widehat{\{f,g\}}^{preQ},$ where $\{\cdot,\cdot\}$ is the Poisson bracket, $[\cdot,\cdot]$ is the operator commutator, and $\hbar=1/k$. \end{enumerate} Indeed, the prequantization (\ref{eqn:K-Squantization}) is derived precisely so that it satisfies (1) -- (3) above. (See \cite[Chap. 8]{Woo}).
nodes.statement_short: Recall that prequantization satisfies Dirac's conditions.

nodes.name: Prequantum space too big
nodes.statement: Unfortunately, the pair $(L^{2}(T^{\ast}M,L_{\Omega}^{\otimes k}),\,f\mapsto\widehat{f}^{preQ})$ does not define a ``good'' quantization, essentially because $L^{2}(T^{\ast}M,L_{\Omega}^{\otimes k})$ is too big. For example, in the case $\omega=0$ and $M=\mathbb{R}^{n}$, which corresponds to a free particle moving in Euclidean space, the line bundle $L_{\Omega}^{\otimes k}$ is trivial and the prequantum Hilbert space is then $L^{2}(T^{\ast}\mathbb{R}^{n}=\mathbb{R}^{n}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}).$ The variables in the first $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ factor give the position of the particle, and the variables in the second $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ factor describe the momentum. But one knows from quantum mechanics that a wave function cannot be simultaneously a function of both position \emph{and} momentum.
nodes.statement_short: Explain why the prequantum Hilbert space is too large.

nodes.name: Vertical polarization
nodes.statement: In order to obtain a Hilbert space of the ``correct'' size, one first chooses a polarization of $(T^*M,\Omega)$. A \emph{polarization} of a symplectic manifold is an integrable (real or complex) Lagrangian distribution. If, as is the case here, the phase space is a cotangent bundle, one may take the \emph{vertical polarization}, i.e., the distribution given by the tangent spaces to the fibers of $T^{\ast}M$. (Note that this distribution is indeed Lagrangian with respect to $\Omega$ as well as $\omega_0$.) This means that we are considering wave functions which depend only on position, not on momentum. Thus, the vertical polarization corresponds to the ``position-space representation'' in quantum mechanics.
nodes.statement_short: Choose the vertical polarization.

nodes.name: Problems with polarized sections
nodes.statement: Once a choice of polarization $\mathcal{P}$ is made, one would ideally like to define the quantum Hilbert space to be the subspace $L^2_\mathcal{P}(T^*M,L_{\Omega}^{\otimes k})$ of the prequantum Hilbert space $L^2(T^*M,L_{\Omega}^{\otimes k})$ consisting of those sections that are covariantly constant in the $\mathcal{P}$ directions and then restrict the Kostant-Souriau prequantum Hamiltonians $\widehat{f}^{preQ}$ to this subspace. However, there are two problems here. First, $L^2_\mathcal{P}=\{0\}$! Secondly, even for a polarization $\mathcal{P}$ that yields a nontrivial quantum Hilbert space,\footnote{A typical example of such a polarization is available whenever $T^*M$ admits a K\"ahler structure, for example when $M$ is a compact Lie group. In this case, one can take $\mathcal{P}$ to be the holomorphic tangent bundle.} the Kostant-Souriau quantization $\widehat{f}^{preQ}$ does not in general preserve the quantum Hilbert space. Indeed, $\widehat{f}^{preQ}$ will only preserve $\mathcal{H}_{k}$ if the Hamiltonian flow of $f$ preserves the polarization $\mathcal{P}$. One can show that the $\Omega$-Hamiltonian flow of $H$ does not preserve \emph{any} polarization.
nodes.statement_short: Polarized sections are trivial and the flow of $H$ preserves no polarization.

nodes.name: Half-form correction
nodes.statement: Fortunately, there is only one more piece of the puzzle which will remedy both of the remaining problems at once: the so-called half-form correction. The half-form correction boils down to tensoring $L^{\otimes k}$ with a square root of the canonical bundle associated to the polarization. Sections of such a bundle are called half-forms. The half-form correction, due essentially to Blattner, Kostant and Sternberg, allows one to quantize a larger set of functions than just those whose flows preserve the polarization, and in particular one can quantize the standard Hamiltonians which appear in wave mechanics, of which our $H=\frac{1}{2}\Vert\xi\Vert^{2}$ is an example. Moreover, the quantum Hilbert space associated to the vertical polarization, in the presence of the half-form correction, will turn out to be just $L^2(M,L^{\otimes k})$, which is exactly what one would naively expect for the position-space representation.\footnote{There are several further advantages, from both the mathematical and physical viewpoints, though they are not relevant to our current purposes. One, which is easy to describe, is that when using the BKS construction to quantize the simple harmonic oscillator (a well-known example from physics), a shift is introduced which results in the physically correct energy spectrum. Specifically, without the BKS construction, one obtains an energy spectrum consisting of integer multiples of $\hbar.$ The physically correct spectrum, which is obtained using the BKS construction, is $\{(n+\frac{1}{2})\hbar:n\in\mathbb{Z\}}$.}
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the half-form correction, which remedies both problems.

nodes.name: BKS half-form corrected Hilbert space
nodes.statement:
The BKS construction in our setting is as follows. (We refer the interested reader to \cite{Woo}, Chap. 9, for more details and proofs; see also \cite{GS}.) Choose a line bundle $\delta$ such that $\delta\otimes\delta= igwedge^{n}TM$ (this is possible because $ igwedge^{n}TM$ is trivializable), and let $
u$ be a section of $\delta$ with $
u^{2}=\operatorname{vol}_g(M),$ where $\operatorname{vol}_g(M)$ is the Riemannian volume form on $M$. Sections of $\delta$ are called half-forms (associated to the vertical polarization), and the half-form corrected quantum Hilbert space is defined to be \[ \widehat{H}_k:=L^{2}_{\mathcal{P}}(T^*M,L_\Omega^{\otimes k}\otimes\pi^*\delta) \] where the inner product is defined by the canonical pairing of half-forms. In particular, a section of $L_\Omegaightarrow T^*M$ which is vertically covariantly constant is uniquely determined by its value on the zero-section $M$, and the inner product of two such sections is therefore given by ootnote{We will abuse notation slightly and not distinguish between $
u$ (or $\operatorname{vol}_g(M)$) and its pullback $\pi^{\ast}
u$ (resp. $\pi^{\ast}\operatorname{vol}_g(M)$).}  egin{equation} \langle s
u,t
uangle = \left( rac{k}{2\pi}ight)^n\int_M s.t\ \operatorname{vol}_g(M). \end{equation} Hence, we see that the quantum Hilbert space associated to the vertical polarization can be identified with $L^2(M,L^{\otimes k}).$
nodes.statement_short: Construct half-forms and identify the corrected quantum Hilbert space with $L^2(M,L^{\otimes k})$.

nodes.name: Evolve and project
nodes.statement: Now that we have the correct quantum Hilbert space, we need to quantize the Hamiltonian flow of the kinetic energy $H$. Let $\rho_{t}$ denote the Hamiltonian flow of $H$ on $T^{\ast}M$. In order to define the quantization of the Hamiltonian $H$, we evolve $\psi\nu$ for a short time (that is, apply $\exp(-ikt\widehat{H}^{preQ})$ to the first factor, and the pull-back $\rho_{t}^{\ast}$ to the second factor), and then project the result back into $\widehat{\mathcal{H}}_{k}.$
nodes.statement_short: Quantize $H$ by evolving half-form sections briefly and projecting back.

nodes.name: Generalized BKS pairing
nodes.statement: The projection is achieved by a generalization of the half-form pairing (\ref{eqn:half-form-pairing}). One can show that the pushforward of the vertical polarization by $\rho_{t}$ is an integrable Lagrangian distribution which is (at least for small $t$) transverse to the vertical polarization. Hence, there exists some function $f_{t}\in C^{\infty}(T^{\ast}M)$ such that $\rho_{t}^{\ast}(\operatorname{vol}_g(M))\wedge\operatorname{vol}_g(M)=f_{t}\Omega^{n}/n!$. The generalized (BKS) half-form pairing is then defined to be \[ \left( \rho_{t}^{\ast}\nu\right) .\nu:=\sqrt{f_{t}}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Define the generalized BKS half-form pairing.

nodes.name: Quantum Hamiltonian as derivative
nodes.statement: This pairing can be shown to be nondegenerate (at least for small $t$), and therefore defines a bijection between $(\exp(-ikt\,\widehat{H}^{preQ})\otimes\rho_{t}^{\ast})\widehat{\mathcal{H}}_{k}$ and $\widehat{\mathcal{H}}_{k}.$ The quantum Hamiltonian $\widehat{Q}_{k}(H)$ is obtained by computing the derivative with respect to $t$, evaluated at $t=0$, of the operator on $\widehat{\mathcal{H}}_{k}$ given by first applying $(\exp(-ikt\widehat{H}^{preQ})\otimes\rho_{t}^{\ast})$ and then projecting the result back into $\widehat{\mathcal{H}}_{k}$ using the BKS pairing. At the end of the day, we are really interested only in sections of $L^{\otimes k};$ thus, we can take a section $\psi$ in $\mathcal{H}_{k},$ multiply it by $\nu$, apply the BKS construction, and write the result in the form $\psi^{\prime}\nu.$ The quantization of the Hamiltonian $H$ is then defined to be $\widehat{H}_{k}\psi:=\psi^{\prime}$. In our case, this yields the expression in Theorem~\ref{hk}.
nodes.statement_short: Differentiate the projected evolution at $t=0$ to get the quantum Hamiltonian of Theorem 2.3.

nodes.name: Almost conjugate subgroups
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a finite group and let ${{\Gamma}_{1}}$ and ${{\Gamma}_{2}}$ be subgroups of $G$. We will say that ${{\Gamma}_{1}}$ is \emph{almost conjugate} to ${{\Gamma}_{2}}$ in $G$ if there is a bijection $\Gamma_1\to\Gamma_2$ carrying each element of $\Gamma_1$ to a conjugate element in $\Gamma_2$; equivalently, each $G$-conjugacy class $[g]_{G}$ intersects ${{\Gamma}_{1}}$ and ${{\Gamma}_{2}}$ in the same number of elements.
differentia: there is a bijection $\Gamma_1\to\Gamma_2$ carrying each element of $\Gamma_1$ to a conjugate element in $\Gamma_2$
nodes.label: def.ac

nodes.name: Sunada's Theorem
nodes.statement: Sunada's Theorem states that if a finite group $G$ acts by isometries on a compact Riemannian manifold $M$ and if ${{\Gamma}_{1}}$ and ${{\Gamma}_{2}}$ are almost conjugate subgroups of $G$ acting freely on $M$, then ${{\Gamma}_{1}}\backslash M$ and ${{\Gamma}_{2}}\backslash M$ are isospectral.
assumptions: a finite group $G$ acts by isometries on a compact Riemannian manifold $M$
${{\Gamma}_{1}}$ and ${{\Gamma}_{2}}$ are almost conjugate subgroups of $G$ acting freely on $M$

nodes.name: Representation-theoretic almost conjugacy and transplantation
nodes.statement: $\text{ }$ \begin{enumerate} \item The almost conjugacy condition is equivalent to a representation theoretic condition as follows. The right multiplication of $G$ on the cosets in ${\Gamma}_{i}{\backslash} G$ gives rise to a natural action of $G$ on the finite-dimensional vector space ${\mathbf{R}}[{\Gamma}_{i}{\backslash} G]$. The subgroups ${{\Gamma}_{1}}$ and ${{\Gamma}_{2}}$ of $G$ are almost conjugate if and only if there exists an isomorphism \[ \tau: {\mathbf{R}}[{{\Gamma}_{1}}{\backslash} G]\to{\mathbf{R}}[{{\Gamma}_{2} }{\backslash} G] \] intertwining the actions of $G$. \item Assume that ${{\Gamma}_{1}}$ and ${{\Gamma}_{2}}$ are almost conjugate in $G$ and let $\tau$ be the intertwining map in (i). Let $W$ be any vector space on which $G$ acts on the right. For $i=1,2$, let $W^{{\Gamma}_{i}}$ be the subspace of vectors fixed by all elements of ${\Gamma}_{i}$. Then $\tau$ gives rise to a linear isomorphism, called ``transplantation'' \[ \mathcal{T}:W^{{{\Gamma}_{2}}}\to W^{{{\Gamma}_{1}}}. \] Transplantation was first introduced in an example in \cite{Bu86} and systematized in \cite{Be92} to give a new proof of Sunada's Theorem; see also \cite{Z}. We are following the presentation in \cite{GMW}. \item Transplantation is functorial: if $V$ and $W$ are right $G$-spaces and $\psi:V\to W$ is a $G$-equivariant map, then the following diagram commutes: \[ \begin{CD} W^{{{\Gamma}_2}} @>{\mathcal{T}_W}>> W^{{{\Gamma}_1}} \\ @V{\psi}VV @VV{\psi}V \\ V^{{{\Gamma}_2}} @>{\mathcal{T}_V}>> V^{{{\Gamma}_1}}\\ \end{CD} \] Moreover, if $W$ is an inner product space and if the $G$ action is unitary, then the transplantation map is unitary. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Almost conjugacy equals an intertwining isomorphism of permutation representations, which yields a functorial (unitary) transplantation map between fixed-vector spaces.
nodes.label: rem.repcond

nodes.name: Spectrum of the bundle Laplacian and Schrodinger operator
nodes.statement:
Given a Hermitian line bundle $L$ over a closed Riemannian manifold~$(M,g)$ and a Hermitian connection~$
abla$ on~$L$ we denote by $\operatorname{	extit{Spec}}(L,
abla,k)$ the spectrum of the associated Laplace operator~$\Delta$ on $C^\infty(M, L^{\otimes k})$ (recall Notation and Remarks~ef{prep}). For a potential $Q\in C^\infty(M)$, we denote by $\operatorname{	extit{Spec}}(Q;L,
abla,k)$ the spectrum of $\Delta+Q$ on $C^\infty(M, L^{\otimes k})$.
nodes.statement_short: $Spec(L,\nabla,k)$ and $Spec(Q;L,\nabla,k)$ are the spectra of $\Delta$ and $\Delta+Q$ on sections of $L^{\otimes k}$.

nodes.name: Sunada theorem for line bundles (Kuwabara variant)
assumptions: Let $(M,g)$ be a compact Riemannian manifold, let $L$ be a Hermitian line bundle over $M$, and let ${\nabla}$ be a Hermitian connection on $L$. Let $G$ be a finite group that acts on $L$ carrying fibers to fibers, preserving $\nabla$, and such that the induced action on $M$ is by isometries.
suppose that ${\Gamma}_{i}$ is a subgroup of $G$ whose action on $M$ is free.
nodes.statement_short: Almost conjugate subgroups acting freely give quotient line bundles isospectral for all tensor powers, also with invariant potentials.
nodes.label: mt

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.4 by transplantation
nodes.statement: For a proof by transplantation, observe that $G$ acts on the right on the space ${C^\infty}(M,{L^{\otimes k}})$ of smooth sections of ${L^{\otimes k}}$ by $(f.g)(x)=g^{-1}.f(g.x)$ for $f\in{C^\infty}(M,{L^{\otimes k}})$, $g\in G$, and $x\in M$. The space ${C^\infty}(M_i,{L_{i}^{\otimes k}})$ of smooth sections of ${L_{i}^{\otimes k}}$ may be identified with the space ${C^\infty}(M,{L^{\otimes k}})^{{\Gamma}_{i}}$ of ${\Gamma}_{i}$-invariant elements of ${C^\infty}(M,{L^{\otimes k}})$. Thus by Remark \ref{rem.repcond}, we obtain a transplantation map $\mathcal{T}:{C^\infty}(M_2,{L_{2}^{\otimes k}})\rightarrow{C^\infty}(M_1,{L_{1}^{\otimes k}})$. Moreover, with this identification, the Schr\"{o}dinger operator $\Delta_{i}+Q$ on ${C^\infty}(M_i,{L_{i}^{\otimes k}})$ (associated with the Riemannian metric on $M_{i}$, the connection ${\nabla}_{i}$, and the potential~$Q$) is the restriction to ${C^\infty}(M,{L^{\otimes k}})^{{\Gamma}_{i}}$ of the Schr\"{o}dinger operator $\Delta+Q$ of ${L^{\otimes k}}$. Since $\Delta$ commutes with the action of $G$ and since $Q$ is $G$-invariant, we may let $\Delta+Q$ play the role of $\psi$ in Remark~\ref{rem.repcond}. It follows that $\mathcal{T}$ intertwines the Schr\"{o}dinger operators $\Delta_{1}+Q$ and $\Delta_{2}+Q$ on ${L_{1}^{\otimes k}}$ and ${L_{2}^{\otimes k}}$, thus proving the theorem.
nodes.statement_short: Transplantation: identify sections on quotients with $\Gamma_i$-invariant sections and apply the intertwining map to the $G$-commuting Schrodinger operator.

nodes.name: G-action on sections
nodes.statement: For a proof by transplantation, observe that $G$ acts on the right on the space ${C^\infty}(M,{L^{\otimes k}})$ of smooth sections of ${L^{\otimes k}}$ by $(f.g)(x)=g^{-1}.f(g.x)$ for $f\in{C^\infty}(M,{L^{\otimes k}})$, $g\in G$, and $x\in M$.
nodes.statement_short: Let $G$ act on sections of $L^{\otimes k}$.

nodes.name: Transplantation map
nodes.statement: The space ${C^\infty}(M_i,{L_{i}^{\otimes k}})$ of smooth sections of ${L_{i}^{\otimes k}}$ may be identified with the space ${C^\infty}(M,{L^{\otimes k}})^{{\Gamma}_{i}}$ of ${\Gamma}_{i}$-invariant elements of ${C^\infty}(M,{L^{\otimes k}})$. Thus by Remark \ref{rem.repcond}, we obtain a transplantation map $\mathcal{T}:{C^\infty}(M_2,{L_{2}^{\otimes k}})\rightarrow{C^\infty}(M_1,{L_{1}^{\otimes k}})$.
nodes.statement_short: Identify quotient sections with invariant sections and obtain transplantation via Remark 3.2.

nodes.name: Operators as restrictions
nodes.statement: Moreover, with this identification, the Schr\"{o}dinger operator $\Delta_{i}+Q$ on ${C^\infty}(M_i,{L_{i}^{\otimes k}})$ (associated with the Riemannian metric on $M_{i}$, the connection ${\nabla}_{i}$, and the potential~$Q$) is the restriction to ${C^\infty}(M,{L^{\otimes k}})^{{\Gamma}_{i}}$ of the Schr\"{o}dinger operator $\Delta+Q$ of ${L^{\otimes k}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Quotient Schrodinger operators are restrictions of $\Delta+Q$.

nodes.name: Intertwining
nodes.statement: Since $\Delta$ commutes with the action of $G$ and since $Q$ is $G$-invariant, we may let $\Delta+Q$ play the role of $\psi$ in Remark~\ref{rem.repcond}. It follows that $\mathcal{T}$ intertwines the Schr\"{o}dinger operators $\Delta_{1}+Q$ and $\Delta_{2}+Q$ on ${L_{1}^{\otimes k}}$ and ${L_{2}^{\otimes k}}$, thus proving the theorem.
nodes.statement_short: By functoriality, transplantation intertwines the operators, giving isospectrality.

nodes.name: Sunada-type quantum equivalence
assumptions: We use the notation and hypotheses of Proposition~\ref{mt}, part~(i).
Let $-i\omega_j$ be the curvature of the connection ${\nabla}_j$ on $L_j$, $j=1,2$.
conclusions: $(M,\omega_1)$ and $(M_2,\omega_2)$ are quantum equivalent with respect to the connections ${\nabla}_1$ and ${\nabla}_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Under the Sunada hypotheses, the quotient magnetic fields are quantum equivalent.
nodes.label: mc

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.5
nodes.statement: We apply part~(ii) of Proposition~\ref{mt} with the scalar curvature $R$ of $M$ in the role of $Q$. Note that $R$ is necessarily $G$-invariant since $G$ acts by isometries on $M$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Proposition 3.4(ii) with the $G$-invariant scalar curvature as potential.

nodes.name: Canonical line bundle
nodes.statement: Let $(M, g, \omega)$ be a K\"ahler manifold of complex dimension $n$. (Here $\omega$ is the K\"ahler form.) The canonical line bundle $L_{M}$ over $M$ is defined to be the $n$th exterior power of the holomorphic cotangent bundle.
differentia: the $n$th exterior power of the holomorphic cotangent bundle

nodes.name: Canonical connection
nodes.statement: Since $M$ is K\"ahler, the Levi-Civita connection on $TM$ commutes with the complex structure and thus defines a holomorphic connection on the holomorphic tangent bundle. This connection gives rise to a holomorphic connection on $L_{M}$ that we will call the \emph{canonical connection}.

nodes.name: X-space
nodes.statement: If $X$ is a simply-connected Hermitian symmetric space of non-compact type and $M$ is a compact locally symmetric space with universal covering $X$, we will call $M$ an $X$-space.

nodes.name: X-spaces are Hodge manifolds; Chern class of the canonical bundle
nodes.statement: Every $X$-space $M$ is a Hodge manifold, i.e., $M$ is a K\"ahler manifold and a suitable real multiple of the K\"ahler form $\omega$ of $M$ represents an integer cohomology class. More precisely, if the metric is rescaled such that $X$ (and hence each $X$-space $M$) has Einstein constant~$-1$ then the Chern class of the canonical bundle $L_{M}$ is $[\omega/2\pi]$ (see~\cite{Ba}, formulas (4.68) and~(4.59); compare also~\cite{We}, p. 219.)
assumptions: the metric is rescaled such that $X$ (and hence each $X$-space $M$) has Einstein constant~$-1$
conclusions: the Chern class of the canonical bundle $L_{M}$ is $[\omega/2\pi]$
nodes.statement_short: X-spaces are Hodge; normalized to Einstein constant $-1$, the canonical bundle has Chern class $[\omega/2\pi]$.

nodes.name: Quantum equivalence of X-spaces (canonical connections)
nodes.statement: As in Remark~\ref{amb}, the notion of ``quantum equivalence'' of $(M_1,\omega_1)$ and $(M_2,\omega_2)$, where the $M_i$ are $X$-spaces and $\omega_i$ their K\"ahler forms, will mean with respect to the canonical connections on the canonical bundles $L_{M_i}$.

nodes.name: Quantum equivalent but not classically equivalent magnetic fields
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be a simply-connected Hermitian symmetric space of noncompact type of real dimension at least four. Then there exist arbitrarily large families of non-isometric $X$-spaces $M_{i}$ such that the $(M_i,\omega_i)$ are all mutually quantum equivalent but not classically equivalent. In fact the phase spaces $(T^*M_i, \Omega_i)$ of the classical Hamiltonian systems are not symplectomorphic {\rm(}or even homeomorphic{\rm)}.
assumptions: Let $X$ be a simply-connected Hermitian symmetric space of noncompact type of real dimension at least four.
conclusions: there exist arbitrarily large families of non-isometric $X$-spaces $M_{i}$ such that the $(M_i,\omega_i)$ are all mutually quantum equivalent but not classically equivalent.
In fact the phase spaces $(T^*M_i, \Omega_i)$ of the classical Hamiltonian systems are not symplectomorphic {\rm(}or even homeomorphic{\rm)}.
nodes.statement_short: Arbitrarily large families of compact quotients of $X$ whose magnetic fields are quantum equivalent but whose phase spaces are not even homeomorphic.
nodes.label: herm

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.6
nodes.statement: D.B. McReynolds \cite{Mcr} showed, using Sunada's Theorem, that for every simp\-ly-con\-nected symmetric space $X$ of non-compact type, there exist arbitrarily large collections of non-isometric $X$-spaces $M_{i}$ whose Laplace-Beltrami operators are mutually isospectral. For each such collection, there exists an $X$-space $M$ and a finite group $G$ of isometries of $M$ such that $M_{i}={{\Gamma}_{i}{\backslash}M}$, where the ${\Gamma}_{i}$ are almost conjugate subgroups of $G$. In the setting that $X$ is Hermitian symmetric, the isometries are holomorphic. Since all holomorphic isometries of $M$ preserve both the canonical bundle and the canonical connection, we can now apply Theorem~\ref{mc} to see that $(M_{i},\omega_{i})$ and $(M_{j},\omega_{j})$ are quantum equivalent for all $i,j$. Mostow Strong Rigidity tells us that the various $M_{i}$ have non-isomorphic fundamental groups, i.e., $M_{i}=\Lambda_{i}{\backslash}X$ with $\Lambda_{i}$ and $\Lambda_{j}$ non-isomorphic discrete uniform subgroups of the group of isometries of $X$ when $i\neq j$. The cotangent bundle $T^{\ast}M_{i}$ is the quotient of the (trivial) bundle $T^{\ast}X$ by the action of $\Lambda_{i}$ and thus the various $T^{\ast}M_{i}$ are also non-homeomorphic.
nodes.statement_short: Use McReynolds' Sunada-type isospectral families and Theorem 3.5; Mostow rigidity gives non-homeomorphic cotangent bundles.

nodes.name: McReynolds' Sunada families
nodes.statement: D.B. McReynolds \cite{Mcr} showed, using Sunada's Theorem, that for every simp\-ly-con\-nected symmetric space $X$ of non-compact type, there exist arbitrarily large collections of non-isometric $X$-spaces $M_{i}$ whose Laplace-Beltrami operators are mutually isospectral. For each such collection, there exists an $X$-space $M$ and a finite group $G$ of isometries of $M$ such that $M_{i}={{\Gamma}_{i}{\backslash}M}$, where the ${\Gamma}_{i}$ are almost conjugate subgroups of $G$.
nodes.statement_short: Take McReynolds' isospectral families, arising from almost conjugate subgroups.

nodes.name: Apply Theorem 3.5
nodes.statement: In the setting that $X$ is Hermitian symmetric, the isometries are holomorphic. Since all holomorphic isometries of $M$ preserve both the canonical bundle and the canonical connection, we can now apply Theorem~\ref{mc} to see that $(M_{i},\omega_{i})$ and $(M_{j},\omega_{j})$ are quantum equivalent for all $i,j$.
nodes.statement_short: Holomorphic isometries preserve canonical bundle and connection, so Theorem 3.5 gives quantum equivalence.

nodes.name: Mostow rigidity: non-homeomorphic cotangent bundles
nodes.statement: Mostow Strong Rigidity tells us that the various $M_{i}$ have non-isomorphic fundamental groups, i.e., $M_{i}=\Lambda_{i}{\backslash}X$ with $\Lambda_{i}$ and $\Lambda_{j}$ non-isomorphic discrete uniform subgroups of the group of isometries of $X$ when $i\neq j$. The cotangent bundle $T^{\ast}M_{i}$ is the quotient of the (trivial) bundle $T^{\ast}X$ by the action of $\Lambda_{i}$ and thus the various $T^{\ast}M_{i}$ are also non-homeomorphic.
nodes.statement_short: Mostow rigidity gives non-isomorphic fundamental groups, hence non-homeomorphic cotangent bundles.

nodes.name: Role of the dimension assumption
nodes.statement: The assumption on the dimension of $X$ in Theorem~\ref{herm}, equivalently the exclusion of the case that $X$ is the real hyperbolic plane, was needed only so that the phase spaces for the classical Hamiltonian systems would not be homeomorphic.

nodes.name: Isospectral hyperbolic Riemann surfaces are quantum equivalent
nodes.statement: Let $(M_1,g_1)$ and $(M_2,g_2)$ be \emph{any} pair of hyperbolic Riemann surfaces which are iso\-spec\-tral with respect to the Laplace-Beltrami operator acting on functions. Then $(M_1,\omega_1)$ and $(M_2,\omega_2)$ are quantum equivalent, where $\omega_i$ is the K\"ahler form of $(M_i,g_i)$.
assumptions: Let $(M_1,g_1)$ and $(M_2,g_2)$ be \emph{any} pair of hyperbolic Riemann surfaces which are iso\-spec\-tral with respect to the Laplace-Beltrami operator acting on functions.
where $\omega_i$ is the K\"ahler form of $(M_i,g_i)$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.7
nodes.statement: H. Pesce \cite{Pes} proved that every pair of isospectral compact Riemann surfaces $(M_1,g_1)$ and $(M_2,g_2)$ is \emph{strongly} isospectral in the following sense: Let $G=PSL(2,{\mathbb{R}})$. A Hermitian vector bundle $E$ over the hyberbolic plane $X$ is said to be homogeneous if $G$ acts on $E$, carrying fibers to fibers, such that the induced action on $X$ is the standard action by isometries. The actions of $G$ on $M$ and $E$ give rise to an action of $G$ on the space of smooth sections of $E$. A self-adjoint elliptic differential operator $D$ on $E$ (i.e., on smooth sections of $E$) is said to be \emph{natural} if it commutes with the $G$-action. In that case, if ${\Gamma}$ is a discrete subgroup of $G$ acting freely and properly discontinuously on $X$, then $D$ induces a self-adjoint elliptic differential operator on the bundle ${\Gamma}{\backslash} E$ over the Riemann surface ${\Gamma}{\backslash} M$. Compact Riemann surfaces $M_1={\Gamma}_1{\backslash} X$ and $M_2={\Gamma}_2{\backslash} X$ are said to be \emph{strongly isospectral} if for each homogeneous Hermitian vector bundle $E$ over $X$ and each natural self-adjoint elliptic operator $D$ on $E$, the induced operators on the bundles ${\Gamma}_1{\backslash} E$ over $M_1$ and ${\Gamma}_2{\backslash} E$ over $M_2$ are isospectral. (Aside: The key point in proving that isospectral compact Riemann surfaces $M_1={\Gamma}_1{\backslash} X$ and $M_2={\Gamma}_2{\backslash} X$ are always strongly isospectral is that isospectrality of the Riemann surfaces implies that the representations of $G$ induced by the trivial representations of ${\Gamma}_1$ and ${\Gamma}_2$ are equivalent. This condition is considerably weaker than the Sunada condition, which requires that ${\Gamma}_1$ and ${\Gamma}_2$ be subgroups of some finite subgroup ${\Gamma}$ of $G$ and that the trivial representations of ${\Gamma}_1$ and ${\Gamma}_2$ induce equivalent representations of ${\Gamma}$.) The proposition follows from that fact that the canonical Hermitian line bundle over $X$ and all its tensor powers are homogeneous, and the Laplacian associated with the canonical connection is natural.
nodes.statement_short: Pesce: isospectral Riemann surfaces are strongly isospectral; the canonical bundle powers are homogeneous and their Laplacian natural.

nodes.name: Pesce's strong isospectrality
nodes.statement: H. Pesce \cite{Pes} proved that every pair of isospectral compact Riemann surfaces $(M_1,g_1)$ and $(M_2,g_2)$ is \emph{strongly} isospectral in the following sense:
nodes.statement_short: Invoke Pesce: isospectral surfaces are strongly isospectral.

nodes.name: Homogeneous bundles
nodes.statement: Let $G=PSL(2,{\mathbb{R}})$. A Hermitian vector bundle $E$ over the hyberbolic plane $X$ is said to be homogeneous if $G$ acts on $E$, carrying fibers to fibers, such that the induced action on $X$ is the standard action by isometries.
nodes.statement_short: Define homogeneous Hermitian vector bundles over $X$.

nodes.name: Natural operators
nodes.statement: The actions of $G$ on $M$ and $E$ give rise to an action of $G$ on the space of smooth sections of $E$. A self-adjoint elliptic differential operator $D$ on $E$ (i.e., on smooth sections of $E$) is said to be \emph{natural} if it commutes with the $G$-action. In that case, if ${\Gamma}$ is a discrete subgroup of $G$ acting freely and properly discontinuously on $X$, then $D$ induces a self-adjoint elliptic differential operator on the bundle ${\Gamma}{\backslash} E$ over the Riemann surface ${\Gamma}{\backslash} M$.
nodes.statement_short: Define natural operators and their induced operators on quotients.

nodes.name: Strong isospectrality
nodes.statement: Compact Riemann surfaces $M_1={\Gamma}_1{\backslash} X$ and $M_2={\Gamma}_2{\backslash} X$ are said to be \emph{strongly isospectral} if for each homogeneous Hermitian vector bundle $E$ over $X$ and each natural self-adjoint elliptic operator $D$ on $E$, the induced operators on the bundles ${\Gamma}_1{\backslash} E$ over $M_1$ and ${\Gamma}_2{\backslash} E$ over $M_2$ are isospectral.
nodes.statement_short: Define strong isospectrality.

nodes.name: Aside on the key point
nodes.statement: (Aside: The key point in proving that isospectral compact Riemann surfaces $M_1={\Gamma}_1{\backslash} X$ and $M_2={\Gamma}_2{\backslash} X$ are always strongly isospectral is that isospectrality of the Riemann surfaces implies that the representations of $G$ induced by the trivial representations of ${\Gamma}_1$ and ${\Gamma}_2$ are equivalent. This condition is considerably weaker than the Sunada condition, which requires that ${\Gamma}_1$ and ${\Gamma}_2$ be subgroups of some finite subgroup ${\Gamma}$ of $G$ and that the trivial representations of ${\Gamma}_1$ and ${\Gamma}_2$ induce equivalent representations of ${\Gamma}$.)
nodes.statement_short: Aside: Pesce's key point is weaker than the Sunada condition.

nodes.name: Canonical bundle is homogeneous
nodes.statement: The proposition follows from that fact that the canonical Hermitian line bundle over $X$ and all its tensor powers are homogeneous, and the Laplacian associated with the canonical connection is natural.
nodes.statement_short: Canonical bundle powers are homogeneous and the Laplacian is natural, so the claim follows.

nodes.name: Isospectral Riemann surfaces beyond Sunada
nodes.statement: Using Sunada's technique, R. Brooks, R. Gornet, and W. Gustafson \cite{BGG} constructed arbitrarily large finite families of mutually isospectral, non-isometric Riemann surfaces. (Their work motivated that of D.B.~McReynolds cited above.) While the vast majority of known isospectral Riemann surfaces were constructed by Sunada's technique, M.-F.~Vign\'eras's examples \cite{V} and recent examples of C.S.~Rajan \cite{R} do not satisfy the Sunada condition.

nodes.name: Isospectral connections and potentials on a single line bundle
nodes.statement: In addition to the hypotheses of Proposition~\ref{mt}, assume that there exists a bundle map $\sigma$ of $L$, projecting to an isometry (also to be denoted $\sigma$) of $M$, such that $\sigma$ normalizes $G$ and such that $\sigma{{\Gamma}_{1}}\sigma^{-1}={{\Gamma}_{2}}$. Continue to denote by $\sigma$ the induced bundle map from ${L_{1}^{\otimes k}}$ to ${L_{2}^{\otimes k}}$. Then \[ {\operatorname{\textit{Spec}}}(Q; L_{1},\nabla_{1},k)={\operatorname{\textit{Spec}}}(\sigma^{*}Q; L_{1},\sigma^{*}\nabla_{2},k) \] for all positive integers $k$.
nodes.section: 4 Isospectral connections and potentials on a line bundle and its tensor powers
assumptions: In addition to the hypotheses of Proposition~\ref{mt},

assume that there exists a bundle map $\sigma$ of $L$, projecting to an isometry (also to be denoted $\sigma$) of $M$, such that $\sigma$ normalizes $G$ and such that $\sigma{{\Gamma}_{1}}\sigma^{-1}={{\Gamma}_{2}}$.
nodes.statement_short: If an isometric bundle map normalizing $G$ conjugates $\Gamma_1$ to $\Gamma_2$, pulling back gives isospectral connections and potentials on $L_1$.
nodes.label: corm

nodes.name: Isospectral potentials
nodes.section: 4 Isospectral connections and potentials on a line bundle and its tensor powers
nodes.statement_short: With a $\sigma$-invariant connection, Corollary 4.1 yields isospectral potentials for the Schrodinger operator.

nodes.name: Brooks' examples of Riemann surfaces with almost conjugate subgroups and outer automorphism
nodes.statement: Brooks ~\cite{Br} gave explicit examples of finite groups~$G$ and Riemann surfaces $(M,g)$ (with a hyperbolic Riemannian metric~$g$) such that the following conditions are satisfied: \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] The group $G$ acts freely by orientation preserving isometries on the oriented Riemann surface $(M,g)$. \item[(ii)] There exists a pair of almost conjugate, nonconjugate subgroups $\Gamma_{1}$, $\Gamma_{2}$ of~$G$. \item[(iii)] There exists an outer automorphism~$\tau$ of~$G$ such that $\Gamma_{2} =\tau\Gamma_{1}\tau^{-1}$ and such that the action of~$G$ extends to a free action of the semi-direct product $\widehat G$ of $G$ and $\langle \tau\rangle$ on~$(M,g)$ by orientation-preserving isometries. \end{itemize}
nodes.section: 4 Isospectral connections and potentials on a line bundle and its tensor powers
conclusions: The group $G$ acts freely by orientation preserving isometries on the oriented Riemann surface $(M,g)$.
There exists a pair of almost conjugate, nonconjugate subgroups $\Gamma_{1}$, $\Gamma_{2}$ of~$G$.

There exists an outer automorphism~$\tau$ of~$G$ such that $\Gamma_{2} =\tau\Gamma_{1}\tau^{-1}$ and such that the action of~$G$ extends to a free action of the semi-direct product $\widehat G$ of $G$ and $\langle \tau\rangle$ on~$(M,g)$ by orientation-preserving isometries.
nodes.statement_short: There exist hyperbolic Riemann surfaces with free isometric $G$-action, almost conjugate nonconjugate subgroups, and an outer automorphism swapping them.

nodes.name: Isospectral connections on Riemann surfaces via Brooks' trick
nodes.section: 4 Isospectral connections and potentials on a line bundle and its tensor powers
nodes.statement_short: Perturb a $\widehat G$-invariant connection by a $G$- but not $\tau$-invariant term to get isospectral connections on $L_1$ for all $k$.
nodes.label: surf

nodes.name: Curvatures of the isospectral connections differ
nodes.section: 4 Isospectral connections and potentials on a line bundle and its tensor powers
nodes.statement_short: The isospectral connections have different curvature, and with a refined choice of $f$ their curvatures are not related by any isometry.
